## Homework

You have a set of 4 .csv files in data/homework. Each file is a timeseries of temperature and light data collected in tide pools in Oregon by Jenn Fields. 

* Bring in all 4 files and calculate the mean and standard deviation of both temperature (Temp.C) and light (Intensity.lux) for each tide pool.

* Use for loop and map() functions in script

## Load Library

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
```

## Reading in the data

### Reading in multiple csvʻs at once

First, test out the data path -->

```{r}
testdata <- read_csv(here("Week_13", "data", "homework", "TP1.csv"))
glimpse(testdata)
```

Next, list files in a directory and set the path "TidePath"

```{r}
# path to the folder on my computer
TidePath <- here("Week_13", "data", "homework")

# List all files in that path matching a pattern, anything with ".csv"
files <- dir(path = TidePath, pattern = ".csv")

files # take a look
```

## for loop

### Pre-allocating space in a data set

```{r}
# One row for each file and 5 columns

oregon_data <- tibble(filename = rep(NA, length(files)), # telling the data set to match the length to assigned file
                    mean_temp = rep(NA, length(files)),
                    temp_sd = rep(NA, length(files)),
                    mean_light = rep(NA, length(files)),
                    light_sd = rep(NA, length(files)))

oregon_data # take a look
```

Testing the first line of code:

```{r}
# Test by reading in the first file
raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(TidePath, "/", files[1]))
head(raw_data)
```
Testing out calculations : 

```{r}
mean_temp <- mean(raw_data$Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE) #test
sd_temp <- sd(raw_data$Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE) # test
mean_temp
sd_temp
```

### Turning it into for loop


```{r}
for (i in seq_along(files)) { # loop over each file (1, 2, 3, 4), reading each file


}
```

Adding it over the raw data files

```{r}
for (i in seq_along(files)) { # filling in the dataframe

  raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(TidePath, "/", files[i])) # what files to load in
  
  oregon_data$filename[i] <- files[i] # assigning the rows
  oregon_data$mean_temp[i] <- mean(raw_data$Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE) # ave. temp
  oregon_data$temp_sd[i]<- sd(raw_data$Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE) # standard deviation
  oregon_data$mean_light[i] <- mean(raw_data$Intensity.lux, na.rm = TRUE) # ave. light
  oregon_data$light_sd[i] <- sd(raw_data$Intensity.lux, na.rm=TRUE) # standard deviation

  oregon_data

}
```

### Creating a plot for every file using for loops

```{r}
file_names <- dir(path = TidePath, pattern = ".csv") # just the file names

for (i in seq_along(file_names)) { # applying the loop to all 4 files
  
    raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(TidePath, "/", file_names[i]), 
                       col_types = cols(Intensity.lux = col_character())) |>
    mutate(Date.Time     = mdy_hm(Date.Time),               # text -> real date-time
           Intensity.lux = parse_number(Intensity.lux))     # "1,032" -> 1032

  site_name <- str_remove(file_names[i], "\\.csv") # drop ".csv" for the title

  p1 <- ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = Date.Time, y = Temp.C, color = Intensity.lux)) + #creating ggplot using 4 data sets
    geom_point() + # geompoint seems to make the most sense
    labs(title = site_name, x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°C)", color = "Light Intensity") #title will change according to file, the x-axis is illegible but I couldnʻt figure out how to get rid of the time.

  ggsave(here("Week_13", "outputs", "for_loops", paste0(site_name, "_temp.png")), # save all plots in this location
         plot = p1, width = 6, height = 4)
}

p1 # preview

```

## purrr map()

Listing files in directory again

```{r}
# path to the folder on my computer
TidePath <- here("Week_13", "data", "homework")

# List all files in that path matching a pattern, anything with ".csv"
files <- dir(path = TidePath, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

files
```

### Read in the files using purrr map()

```{r}
data <- files |>
  set_names() |> # names each list element with its file name
  map(read_csv) |> # a list of 4 dataframes/tibble
  list_rbind(names_to = "filename") # stack them; list names go in a "filename" column, has the entire name

data
```

### Calculate mean and standard deviation for temperature and light using map()

```{r}
data <- files |>
  set_names() |>
  map(read_csv) |> # reading in multiple data using map()
  list_rbind(names_to = "filename") |>
  group_by(filename) |> # applying these calculations to each dataset
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE),
            temp_sd = sd(Temp.C, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_light = mean(Intensity.lux, na.rm = TRUE),
            light_sd = sd(Intensity.lux, na.rm = TRUE))

data
```

### Creating multiple plots at once using map()

```{r}
file_names <- dir(path = TidePath, pattern = ".csv") # just the file names

save_temp_plot <- function(file_name) {
  site_name <- str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv")

   p2 <- read_csv(paste0(TidePath, "/", file_name),
                 col_types = cols(Intensity.lux = col_character())) |> 
    mutate(Date.Time     = mdy_hm(Date.Time),             # for this method, need a different way of eliminating times
           Intensity.lux = parse_number(Intensity.lux)) |> # "1,032" gets rid of the comma, only takes number
    ggplot(aes(x = Date.Time, y = Temp.C, color = Intensity.lux)) + # ^ should do that for everything...
    geom_point() + # exact same plots as before
    scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 day", date_labels = "%b %d") +  # one label per day, no time
    labs(title = site_name, x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°C)", color = "Light Intensity") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
   
 ggsave(here("Week_13", "outputs", "map", paste0(site_name, "_temp.png")),
         plot = p2, width = 6, height = 4)
}

walk(file_names, save_temp_plot) # these plots still came out looking very confusing

```

## Conclusion: 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tp
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and standard deviation of temperature and light in Oregon tide pools"

pool_table <- oregon_data |>
  mutate(filename = parse_number(filename)) |>   # Leaves only the number, "1-4"
  kable(
    col.names = c("Tidepool", "Mean temp (°C)", "SD temp",
                  "Mean light (lux)", "SD light")
  )|>
 kable_minimal() |>
  kable_styling(position = "center")
  

pool_table
```


Both methods of "for loops" and "map()" were useful and efficient ways to work with multiple datasets at once. 
I preferred map() for the initial gathering and calculating of data since it didnʻt require the step of "allocating space" before hand, however, when it came to the plots, I could not figure out how to mutate the x-axis Date.Time labels. Overall, they both allowed for a more efficient way to work with multiple datasets at once.
